question.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=6(x+5)\sqrt[3]{{y}^{2}}$ for $y\ne 0.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =6(x+5)\sqrt[3]{{y}^{2}} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2(x+5)\cdot 3\sqrt[3]{{y}^{2}} \\ \frac{1}{3\sqrt[3]{{y}^{2}}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2(x+5)\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{3\sqrt[3]{{y}^{2}}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int 2(x+5)\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{3\sqrt[3]{{y}^{2}}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int 2(x+5)\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{3\sqrt[3]{{y}^{2}}}\cdot \text{d}y & =\int 2(x+5)\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{3}\int {y}^{-2/3}\,\text{d}y & =\int 2(x+5)\,\text{d}x \\ {y}^{1/3} & ={(x+5)}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
{y}^{1/3}={(x+5)}^{2}+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
y=({(x+5)}^{2}+C)^{3}.
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡|T-15| & =-0.04t+C \\ |T-15| & ={e}^{-0.04t+C} \\ |T-15| & =K\,{e}^{-0.04t}\end{aligned}
$$

where $K={e}^{C}$ is an arbitrary positive constant.

We can drop the absolute value bars by allowing $K$ to be both positive and negative. Therefore, the most general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =15+K\,{e}^{-0.04t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here $K$ is arbitrary and nonzero.
